analysis.one_liner: Repeals the USA PATRIOT Act and major FISA surveillance powers and requires warrants to spy on Americans.
analysis.headline: Introduced with a single cosponsor in the last weeks of 2020 and referred to eight House committees, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard's bill would have repealed the USA PATRIOT Act and the FISA Amendments Act of 2008, required a probable-cause warrant before the government collected information on any American, banned government-mandated backdoors into phone and computer encryption, and protected intelligence community whistleblowers from retaliation. It was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced, December 15, 2020, and none of them ever acted on it. The bill expired when the 116th Congress ended three weeks later.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose phone calls, emails, and online activity are swept up under the surveillance laws the bill repeals: it would require a warrant based on probable cause before the government targeted a U.S. person under FISA or Executive Order 12333, and would require destruction of previously collected information on Americans not tied to an active investigation. Tech companies that make phones and software would benefit from a ban on forced encryption backdoors, and intelligence employees and contractors would gain protection from retaliation for reporting waste, fraud, or lawbreaking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: American phone and internet users; whistleblowers

how_it_helps.text: Bars the government from targeting a U.S. person under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act or Executive Order 12333 without a valid warrant based on probable cause, and requires destruction of information on Americans collected under the repealed laws or without a warrant that is not tied to an active investigation.

Repeals the USA PATRIOT Act and all but two provisions of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008, eliminating the statutory basis for programs that collect Americans' communications, including the Section 702 program.
Prohibits the federal government from forcing electronics or software makers to build a mechanism that lets the government bypass encryption or privacy technology on consumer devices.

Protects intelligence community employees and contractors from retaliation for reporting violations of law, gross waste, or dangers to public safety to Congress, the Comptroller General, or the Inspector General, with administrative sanctions up to termination for retaliators.

Adds outside oversight: annual Government Accountability Office audits of compliance with FISA and Executive Order 12333, authority for the surveillance court to appoint technically expert special masters, and longer terms for its judges.

analysis.who_pays: The intelligence community and federal law enforcement would lose surveillance authorities they have operated under since 2001 and 2008, including the Section 702 program, and would bear the cost of destroying previously collected data on Americans. Supporters of current law would say counterterrorism and counterintelligence investigations would be harder without these tools; the bill contains no replacement framework, only repeal plus a blanket warrant requirement.

drawbacks.text: The repeal is a blunt instrument: it eliminates all of the FISA Amendments Act and the USA PATRIOT Act at once, including authorities used against foreign terrorists and spies abroad, without a tailored replacement framework, which national security officials would argue handicaps legitimate foreign intelligence work.

The mandated destruction of previously collected information on Americans not tied to an active investigation could also erase records that congressional or court reviewers might use to audit past programs and past abuses.

Extending surveillance court judges' terms from seven to ten years and making them eligible for reappointment reduces turnover on a court that civil liberties critics already viewed as too deferential to the government, since reappointment gives the appointing Chief Justice continued leverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For privacy, the bill is close to the maximal position: repeal the two big surveillance statutes, require warrants for spying on Americans, ban encryption backdoors, and shield whistleblowers. The genuine cost is that it repeals first and asks questions later — there is no calibrated replacement for legitimate foreign intelligence collection, and national security agencies would lose tools they use against non-American targets. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill was written as a statement of principle rather than a workable transition, which is one reason it drew no committee interest even from civil-liberties-minded members.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 116th Congress and sent to eight committees; none of them held a hearing or markup, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard introduced the bill on December 15, 2020, in the lame-duck period after the November election, with Rep. Thomas Massie as its only cosponsor.

The same day, the House referred it to eight committees — Judiciary, Intelligence, Financial Services, Foreign Affairs, Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Armed Services — a multi-committee referral that requires sustained interest in multiple panels to overcome.
No committee ever reported the bill, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled in the roughly three weeks before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence community and the executive branch came out ahead by default: every surveillance authority the bill would have repealed — the USA PATRIOT Act and the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 — remained on the books unchanged, and no member had to cast a recorded vote on warrantless surveillance of Americans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The intelligence community and the surveillance status quo

for.name: Tulsi Gabbard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 15, 2020, the only step anyone took to advance it.

for.name: Thomas Massie
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan two-member effort with no additional support.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.role: Chair, House Judiciary Committee (the lead committee of referral)
against.what_they_did: His committee, like all eight committees of referral, never held a hearing or markup on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so the partisan split was never tested; its only two backers were one Democrat (Gabbard) and one Republican (Massie), and no other member of either party signed on.

industries.note: The bill would strip the core statutory authorities these agencies operate under — the USA PATRIOT Act, the FISA Amendments Act including Section 702, and warrantless targeting under Executive Order 12333 — and require destruction of data previously collected on Americans. Their institutional interest in preserving those powers runs directly against the privacy interest of ordinary people.

The bill bans the government from forcing device or software makers to build backdoors around encryption, which the industry has uniformly resisted because a mandated weakness exposes every customer, not just investigation targets. Its interest here lines up with users' privacy.
